newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris anti-smog plan to hit foreign cars.
newsitem.headline: Paris anti-smog plan to hit foreign cars.

text.p: France will ban half of all cars, including foreign-registered vehicles, from Paris when air pollution threatens the capital, Environment Minister Corinne Lepage said on Wednesday.
Giving details of an anti-smog plan announced on Tuesday, Lepage said public transport would be free of charge in Paris on days with the car ban and that offenders risked stiff fines.

Lepage, who had originally said the curbs would take effect when top levels of pollution were reached, told reporters that the ban would be imposed on the basis of forecasts for the following day, making it more frequent.

The worst level of smog under a three-stage measuring system has been reached only twice in Paris, in 1995. The second stage is reached a handful of times a year -- most recently on Monday when Paris cut the speed limit and freed up parking.
Lepage said she might well have imposed the car ban for Tuesday, even though an unexpected breeze cleared Monday's smog, caused by car exhausts on an unusually still and warm spring day.

"The new measures may be taken when the second level of the alert procedure is passed, when there is a risk of reaching the third level the next day," she told reporters while inspecting police environmental checks on vehicles in central Paris.

Under the scheme, vehicles with an even number at the end of a first cluster of digits in the licence plate would be banned from the roads of the capital on smog-filled days of months containing an even number of days. The same would apply to odd numbers.
Apart from emergency vehicles like ambulances and fire engines, commercial vehicles, buses, taxis, electric vehicles and cars with more than three people aboard would be exempt.
Tourists in foreign-registered vehicles would be covered by the ban, said Lepage, accompanied by Paris Mayor Jean Tiberi and Paris police chief Philippe Massoni.
Once the city got used to the curbs, offenders would be forced to leave their cars and pay fines of up to 900 francs ($160).
